family_judgments.evidence: The transformation item has a blocking exact-key failure for ordinary pronoun/noun-phrase variants, unlike the constrained and selected-response items.
All formats preserve the requirement to select MUST and form HAVE + participle; no format supplies the target sequence verbatim.
Each format concerns a confident deduction that Nina took the missing spare key earlier.

criteria.evidence: The blank requires modal MUST plus perfect HAVE and irregular participle taken.
The deduction context is necessary to interpret MUST and adds no major undeclared response grammar.
Neither must nor the perfect sequence is supplied in the response slot.
The required modal and lemma, plus the past-evidence context, constrain “must have taken”; the contraction is accepted.
Both full and contracted forms are accepted, and no unkeyed alternative was proposed.
The irregular participle taken contributes lexical-morphology burden alongside the target modal-perfect construction.
The reply requires MUST + HAVE + TAKEN, directly engaging both declared KCs.
The dialogue only supplies evidence for the intended epistemic deduction.
The response form is not supplied by the dialogue or cue.
The missing-key evidence and mandatory must/take cue select the intended modal perfect, including the accepted contraction.
The key includes the full and contracted target forms; no solver proposed a further reasonable completion.
The learner must track evidential reasoning and an irregular participle in addition to the grammar target.
A is distinguished from omission of the perfect, base-form take, and weaker might; it represents both modal MUST and perfect HAVE.
The options use a common lexical frame and the context supports the intended deduction.
Recognition and the visibly malformed base-form distractor allow some testwise elimination, though the must-versus-might semantic contrast remains relevant.
A is the uniquely strongest deduction under the instruction and supplied evidence.
A is the only keyed option and no reasonable unkeyed option was proposed.
Selecting MUST rather than MIGHT requires pragmatic strength-of-inference judgment in addition to form recognition.
The learner must construct MUST + HAVE + TAKEN from the lemmas must and take, so both declared operations remain active.
The source statements establish the deduction and do not impose a further grammatical transformation.
The cue does not provide HAVE or TAKEN, so the modal-perfect sequence must be formed.
“Nina must have taken it” and “Nina must have taken the key” are natural responses in the supplied key context.
Reasonable contextually resolved alternatives such as “Nina must have taken it” are unaccepted; the prompt requires must and take but not the exact noun phrase.
Open production adds referential-choice and inference burden beyond forming the modal perfect.

summary: The modal-perfect target is active across formats, but the open transformation rejects reasonable referential variants such as “Nina must have taken it.”
